results.main_text_excerpt: Piano scales for beginners Start with one scale, one hand and one octave. Check the notes before adding a steady beat, then finish with one specific detail to revisit. Start with one task A useful practice session ends with something specific to remember: a note you corrected, a fingering you checked or a setting to use next time. You do not need to work through every scale in one sitting. Use this guide alongside the piano scale chart , rather than treating a long list of keys as a daily assignment. Choose one clear starting point For a first reference, open C major . Its ascending notes are C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C . In the right-hand reference, C4 to C5 is one octave. The last C is a higher occurrence of the starting note, not a new eighth scale degree. The major-scale step pattern is whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half. Use the note names, keyboard and staff together. The keyboard shows where a sound is played; the staff and labels preserve its written name and register. When you change direction, read the new sequence instead of assuming the display is unchanged. Already practicing another scale? Open that scale directly. Read its form, hand, direction and range before using the finger numbers. Check the form before practicing minor A minor contains three references here. A natural minor uses A-B-C-D-E-F-G. Harmonic minor raises G to G♯. In the classical melodic-minor scale exercise, the ascent raises F and G; the descent returns to the natural-minor collection. C major shares its note collection with A natural minor , not with all three forms. The classical exercise convention is not a rule that every melody must lower those notes whenever it descends.
